notes:
Here are verse-by-verse notes on 1 Kings 5, drawn from the sources I was able to access within search and fetch limits. I have noted where certain tradition-specific resources or alternative views could not be retrieved.

---

## Overview

The chapter has two main sections: Solomon’s correspondence with Hiram of Tyre to secure timber (vv. 1–12), and Solomon’s organisation of the labour force for the temple project (vv. 13–18). The parallel account is in 2 Chronicles 2, which supplies extra details such as Solomon’s request for a skilled Tyrian artisan. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-5-commentary, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-5.html)

---

## v. 1 — Hiram Sends Envoys to Solomon

**Now when Hiram king of Tyre heard that Solomon had been anointed king in his father’s place, he sent envoys to Solomon; for Hiram had always been a friend of David.**

Hiram (also called Huram in Chronicles) was a Phoenician king ruling the wealthy port-city of Tyre. He had previously supplied David with cedar, carpenters, and stonemasons for David’s palace (2 Sam. 5:11). The Hebrew word for “friend” is *aheb* (LXX: *agapao*), literally “loved” — Hiram had a genuine, long-standing affection for David. The embassy here was one of condolence over David’s death and congratulation on Solomon’s accession. Solomon’s later partnership with Hiram was therefore built on David’s godly influence on this foreign king. David’s life had a “ripple effect” continuing beyond the grave. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-5-commentary, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-5/, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-5.html)

Josephus (Antiquities 8.2.8) claimed that copies of the letters between Solomon and Hiram were preserved in both Hebrew and Tyrian archives and were still extant in his day. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-5/)

---

## v. 2 — Solomon Replies

**And Solomon relayed this message to Hiram:**

Solomon sent a written reply, probably by his own ambassadors (Gill). This exchange marked the formal start of negotiations for temple materials. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-5.html)

---

## v. 3 — David Could Not Build the Temple

**“As you are well aware, due to the wars waged on all sides against my father David, he could not build a house for the Name of the LORD his God until the LORD had put his enemies under his feet.”**

Solomon assumes Hiram already knows this — perhaps because David himself had shared his spiritual aspirations with Hiram. David spoke to this pagan king “as if Hiram were already an Israelite” (Guzik). The phrase “house for the Name of the LORD” is rooted in Deut. 12:5, 11 — the place where God would cause His name to dwell. The “Name” (*shem*) signifies God’s reputation, character, and self-revelation. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-5/, https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-5-commentary)

“Until the LORD put them under the soles of his feet” — this is symbolic language for total conquest. In ancient Near Eastern art, enemies were depicted as a footstool (cf. Psalm 110:1). The verse illustrates the dynamic of God’s sovereignty (“the LORD put…”) and human responsibility (David fought the wars). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-5/, https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-5-commentary)

1 Chronicles 22:8 and 28:3 give the fuller reason: God forbade David because he was “a man of war” who had “shed much blood.” MacLaren notes that a divine decorum forbade a warlike king from being the temple-builder in Israel, unlike in Assyria and Egypt where warrior-kings built the great temples. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-5-commentary, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mac/1-kings-5.html)

---

## v. 4 — Solomon’s Rest

**“But now the LORD my God has given me rest on every side, and there is no adversary or crisis.”**

Solomon recognises his rest as a gift of grace from God, not his own achievement. He calls the LORD “my God,” echoing David in the previous verse who said “his God.” MacLaren observes: “The son had inherited the divine protection and the father’s sense of personal relation to Jehovah. That is a better legacy than a throne.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mac/1-kings-5.html, https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-5-commentary)

The Hebrew word for “adversary” is literally *satan*. The Latin Vulgate translates “nor a Satan.” At this stage in Israel’s history, *satan* functioned as a common noun meaning “adversary” or “opponent”; it was only later personalised (1 Chron. 21:1; Job 1:6). Solomon began his reign with no *satan*, but by 1 Kings 11:14, 23 the LORD raised up adversaries against him. The “rest” fulfilled God’s promise in Deut. 12:10 and Exod. 33:14. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-5/, https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-5-commentary, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-5.html)

MacLaren adds: “We are often more ready to recognise God’s hand in sorrows than in joys… The effect of blessings should be thankfulness, and the proof of thankfulness is service.” Solomon did not take his prosperity as an excuse for luxurious ease but as God’s call to a great task. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mac/1-kings-5.html)

---

## v. 5 — Solomon’s Purpose: To Build a House for the Name of the LORD

**“So behold, I plan to build a house for the Name of the LORD my God, according to what the LORD said to my father David: ‘I will put your son on your throne in your place, and he will build the house for My Name.’”**

The word “behold” (*hinneh*) is a divine highlighter — Spurgeon called it “a word of wonder… intended to excite admiration.” (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-5-commentary)

Solomon grounds his project not in personal ambition but in God’s explicit promise (2 Sam. 7:12–13). MacLaren contrasts this with ancient pagan temple-builders whose motives were “largely ostentation and the wish to outdo predecessors.” Solomon was moved by thankfulness and obedience. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mac/1-kings-5.html)

The phrase “house for the Name of the LORD” (rather than “house for the LORD”) is deliberate. Pagans believed their temples were the actual residence of their gods. Solomon knew “the heaven of heavens could not contain Him, much less this house” (MacLaren, quoting 1 Kings 8:27). The temple was to be the place of God’s self-revelation (*Shekinah*), not His containment. Gill notes that Solomon’s work typifies Christ, the builder of His church (Zech. 6:12). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mac/1-kings-5.html, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-5.html, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-5/)

---

## v. 6 — Solomon Requests Cedar and Skilled Labour

**“Now therefore, order that cedars of Lebanon be cut down for me. My servants will be with your servants, and I will pay your servants whatever wages you set, for you know that there are none among us as skilled in logging as the Sidonians.”**

The cedars of Lebanon were proverbial for their beauty, fragrance, and durability (Song 4:11; Ps. 104:16). The central range of Lebanon is bare, but the lower ranges once had magnificent forests of which only a small remnant survives today. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-5.html)

Solomon sought the best materials possible for God’s house. He also shows humility in acknowledging Israel’s lack of skill: the Sidonians (Phoenicians) were famed throughout the ancient world as timber craftsmen. The Palermo Stone (c. 2200 BC) already records timber-carrying ships from Byblos to Egypt. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-5/)

Gill raises an interesting question: Did the cedar trees actually belong to Solomon (Lebanon being partly within Israel’s borders) or to Hiram? He notes that Solomon pays for labour but initially makes no mention of paying for the timber itself, which “seems to countenance the notion that the trees were Solomon’s.” Yet the massive food payments (v. 11) probably served as an equivalent for the timber as well. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-5.html)

Solomon’s willingness to use Gentile wood and Gentile labour for the temple is significant. Trapp noted: “Only Jews built the tabernacle, but the temple is not built without the aid of the Gentile Tyrians. They, together with us, make up the Church of God.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-5/)

---

## v. 7 — Hiram Rejoices and Blesses the LORD

**When Hiram received Solomon’s message, he rejoiced greatly and said, “Blessed be the LORD this day! He has given David a wise son over this great people!”**

Hiram’s response shows genuine warmth and deference. In the fuller account of 2 Chron. 2:12–16, his acknowledgment of Jehovah is even more marked. Ellicott, however, cautions: Hiram’s blessing of the LORD “is a token rather of such deference to Israel, than of any acceptance of Him as the one true God.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-5.html)

Gill similarly says Hiram “seems to have some knowledge of the true God, the God of Israel, and might worship Him, though along with him other deities, as some Heathen princes did.” Guzik puts it: “We can’t say if Hiram was a saved man, but he certainly respected the God of Israel.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-5/, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-5.html)

The joy and blessing are attributable to David’s godly influence on Hiram over the years. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-5-commentary)

---

## vv. 8–9 — Hiram’s Reply: Timber by Sea

**Then Hiram sent a reply to Solomon, saying: “I have received your message; I will do all you desire regarding the cedar and cypress timber. My servants will haul the logs from Lebanon to the Sea, and I will float them as rafts by sea to the place you specify. There I will separate the logs, and you can take them away. And in exchange, you can meet my needs by providing my household with food.”**

Hiram agrees to supply both cedar and cypress (“fir” in older translations — Ellicott says it is almost certainly cypress). The logs would be hauled from the Lebanon forests down to the Mediterranean coast, bound into rafts, and floated to the location Solomon designated — Joppa, according to 2 Chron. 2:16. From Joppa the timber was carried about 40 miles inland to Jerusalem. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-5.html, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-5.html)

Hiram asks only for “food for my household” in return. MacLaren notes that the narrow coastal strip of Tyre could not grow enough food for its population; it was historically dependent on Palestine for grain (cf. Acts 12:20; Ezra 3:7). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mac/1-kings-5.html)

---

## vv. 10–11 — The Exchange: Timber for Food

**So Hiram provided Solomon with all the cedar and cypress timber he wanted, and year after year Solomon would provide Hiram with 20,000 cors of wheat as food for his household, as well as 20,000 baths of pure olive oil.**

The *cor* (or *kor*) was a Hebrew dry measure equal to about 10 ephahs — roughly 75 gallons or more. Twenty thousand cors of wheat was a vast annual supply. The oil figure presents a textual question: 1 Kings reads “twenty baths” (which MacLaren calls “impossibly small”), while the Septuagint and 2 Chron. 2:10 read “twenty thousand baths.” Most commentators accept the larger figure as original. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mac/1-kings-5.html, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-5.html)

The “pure olive oil” (*beaten oil*) was oil from olives crushed without pressing — the finest grade, fitting for a royal household. Hiram did not take unfair advantage of Solomon’s open-ended offer (“whatever wages you set,” v. 6). His request was reasonable and practical. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-5/)

MacLaren, however, offers a pointed observation: Hiram may have been friendly, but “he was too true a Phoenician not to drive a good bargain… ‘Nothing for nothing’ seems to have been his motto.” Solomon, by contrast, shows “uncalculating lavishness” — “all for love, and nothing for reward.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mac/1-kings-5.html)

---

## v. 12 — Wisdom, Peace, and Treaty

**And the LORD gave Solomon wisdom, as He had promised him. There was peace between Hiram and Solomon, and the two of them made a treaty.**

This verse directly connects Solomon’s diplomatic success with God’s promised gift of wisdom (1 Kings 3:12). The Pulpit Commentary notes that peace is “one fruit of the gift” (cf. James 3:17). The Hebrew for “made a treaty” is literally “cut a covenant” — referring to the ancient practice of ratifying covenants by cutting sacrificial animals and passing between the pieces (Gen. 15:18; Jer. 34:18–19). (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/5.htm)

Gill adds that Solomon “might lawfully do” this because the Tyrians were not among the seven Canaanite nations with whom Israel was forbidden to make alliances (Deut. 7:1–2). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-5.html)

Dr. Constable (Dallas Theological Seminary) notes that “when a person’s ways please the LORD, He makes even his enemies to be at peace with him” (Prov. 16:7) — this was God’s blessing on Solomon at this season. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-5.html — excerpt from search)

---

## v. 13 — Conscription of 30,000 Israelites

**Then King Solomon conscripted a labor force of 30,000 men from all Israel.**

The Hebrew *vayya‘al* literally means “caused to go up” — a levy, not of money but of men. These 30,000 were Israelites (not Canaanite slaves), conscripted for temporary service. The Preacher’s Complete Homiletical Commentary distinguishes these from the Canaanite bondservants of 1 Kings 9:20–22 and the prisoners of war David had taken. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/1-kings-5.html, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-5.html)

The sheer scale of the labour force shows that the temple could only be built during a time of national peace and prosperity — the fruit of David’s conquests and Solomon’s peace. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-5/)

---

## v. 14 — The Shift System

**He sent them to Lebanon in monthly shifts of 10,000 men, so that they would spend one month in Lebanon and two months at home. And Adoniram was in charge of the forced labor.**

Solomon’s wisdom is visible in his management: he rotated the workforce so each man worked only four months per year in the demanding conditions of Lebanon, with eight months at home attending to family and domestic affairs. This humane arrangement contrasts with the relentless slave-labour typical of ancient royal building projects. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-5/, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-5.html)

Adoniram (also called Adoram) was the same official over tribute / forced labour mentioned in 1 Kings 4:6. He would later be stoned to death by the northern tribes when Rehoboam sent him to enforce conscription (1 Kings 12:18), suggesting the system, however wisely administered in Solomon’s day, eventually bred resentment. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-5/, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-5.html)

---

## v. 15 — Porters and Stonecutters

**Solomon had 70,000 porters and 80,000 stonecutters in the mountains,**

These 150,000 workers were distinct from the 30,000 Israelites of v. 13. They were foreigners — Canaanite bondservants (1 Kings 9:20–22; 2 Chron. 8:7–9) and possibly prisoners captured in David’s wars. The porters carried quarried stone from the mountains to Jerusalem; the stonecutters (or “hewers”) extracted and squared the stones on site. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-5.html, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-5/)

Gill observes that the number of Gentile workers (150,000) far exceeded the Israelites (30,000), and sees in this an emblem: “it may denote the greater number of Gentiles in the Gospel church state.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-5.html)

---

## v. 16 — The 3,300 Foremen

**not including his 3,300 foremen who supervised the workers.**

The 3,300 were the “middle management” over the labourers. A well-known numerical question arises: 2 Chron. 2:18 gives 3,600 overseers. Gill harmonises this by noting that 3,300 were the master workmen and 300 were commanders over them, totalling 3,600. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-5.html, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-5/)

---

## v. 17 — Large, Costly Foundation Stones

**And the king commanded them to quarry large, costly stones to lay the foundation of the temple with dressed stones.**

The Hebrew literally speaks of “great stones, costly stones” — not gems but high-quality, dressed (hewn and smoothed) stone, such as marble or porphyry. The key point is that these were foundation stones, hidden from view once the temple was built. Yet Solomon spared no expense or effort even on what nobody would see. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-5.html, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-5/)

This has been a rich source of devotional application. Spurgeon urged that “all our work for God should be done thoroughly, and especially that part of it which lies lowest, and is least observed of men.” He also saw it as a picture of God’s hidden work in believers: “We have been the subjects of a great deal of secret, unseen, underground work… All those chastenings, humblings, and searchings of heart have been a private laying of foundations for higher things.” And for the church corporately: “To maintain solid truth you need solid people. Vital godliness is therefore to be aimed at.” (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-5/)

---

## v. 18 — The Gebalites and Joint Preparation

**So Solomon’s and Hiram’s builders, along with the Gebalites, quarried the stone and prepared the timber and stone for the construction of the temple.**

The “Gebalites” (KJV: “stone-squarers”) were the inhabitants of Gebal (also called Byblos), a Phoenician coastal city north of Sidon. Ezekiel 27:9 mentions the “ancients of Gebal” as skilled ship-caulkers for Tyre. The NIV/NET render it “men from Byblos.” The KJV’s “stone-squarers” is actually a gloss on the proper name, based on the context showing they were skilled in stonework. Ellicott calls this rendering “a curious gloss.” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-5.html, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-5/)

The verse shows a striking international cooperation: Israelites, Tyrians, and Giblites working together to prepare materials for the temple of the God of Israel. Gill again sees “an emblem of the Gentiles concerned in the building of the spiritual temple, the church of Christ” (Zech. 6:15). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-5.html)

---

## Denominational & Tradition-Specific Perspectives

While I was unable to retrieve dedicated resources from all denominational traditions within the search limits, several tradition-distinctive emphases are visible in what was found:

- **Baptist (Calvinistic) — Gill:** Sees Solomon as a type of Christ building His church; stresses that the treaty with Hiram was lawful because Tyre was not among the seven forbidden nations; notes the Gentiles’ large share in temple labour as foreshadowing Gentile predominance in the church. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-5.html)

- **Baptist (General) — Garner-Howes:** The stress falls on practical lessons: “God will make those willing to help who are needed in accomplishment of His appointed tasks (2 Cor. 8:1–4)” and “manifestation of the Lord in one’s life commends him to others (Matt. 5:16).” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/1-kings-5.html — excerpt from search)

- **Charismatic / Evangelical — Enduring Word (Guzik):** Highlights the word *satan* in v. 4 as a spiritual reality, draws strong devotional applications from the hidden foundation stones (Spurgeon), and sees Gentile involvement as a picture of the church. Emphasises the work of God in the “deep and hidden things” of the believer’s life. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-5/)

- **Devotional / Expositional — MacLaren (Broadly Reformed-Baptist):** Stresses the personal relationship with God (“my God”), the proper use of prosperity for God’s service rather than selfish ease, and the contrast between Solomon’s lavish generosity and Hiram’s commercial calculation. MacLaren also insists that the age of building physical temples is past — Christ is the true temple. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mac/1-kings-5.html)

- **Precept Austin (Evangelical / Dispensational-leaning):** Provides detailed Hebrew and Septuagint word studies; emphasizes “the paradoxical principle of 100% dependent and 100% responsible” from v. 3; ties Solomon’s rest to the believer’s rest in Christ (Matt. 11:28–30). (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-5-commentary)

---

## Other Views

- **NET Bible Notes (Modern Scholarship):** Two notes were accessible. (1) The verse numbering in the English Bible from 1 Kings 4:21 through 5:18 differs from the Hebrew text (BHS), where 4:21 ET = 5:1 HT through 5:18 ET = 5:32 HT. (2) The word “name” sometimes refers to one’s reputation or honour and sometimes “designates the LORD himself, being indistinguishable from the proper name.” (https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-5-commentary)

- **Catholic and Orthodox readings:** I was unable to search these sources (newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org) within the available search limit and therefore cannot report on them here.

- **Prosperity / Word of Faith / Hyper-Grace readings:** No relevant material from those viewpoints was encountered in the accessible searches.

---

## Summary of the Chapter’s Message

Solomon, resting in the peace God had given, set about fulfilling the divine purpose for his reign: to build the temple. He did so with wisdom — securing the finest materials through an existing friendship, paying fairly, managing labour humanely, and refusing to cut corners even on the hidden foundations. The chapter portrays a king at his best: grateful, obedient, generous, and wise. The international cooperation foreshadows the inclusion of Gentiles in the spiritual temple of Christ. (Compiled from all sources above.)
